s13p.slug: WEDNESDAY · 9:05 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, THE PORCH — THE SWING
s13p.music: Townes Van Zandt — “If I Needed You”
body: The porch light is off, so the porch gets the living room instead: a long yellow panel through the screen door, laid across the boards and up one leg of the swing. Tomás has a record on in there, low. One man and a guitar, and a voice for the last person still awake in the house. Three doors down a party is losing at beer pong at the top of its lungs, and under all of it the surf comes in at the foot of the bluff and drags its gravel back out.

Skye is on the swing in a ski jacket that has never seen snow, zipped to the chin, her knees pulled up inside it and her hair down. When she sees him at the foot of the steps she pats the empty half of the seat.
“Here,” she says. “That was the rule. And then you come back *here*. I gave you the address.”

He sits, and the swing takes him and sways and settles. She unzips the jacket far enough to get her hands out, takes both of his, and lays all four out on her knees in the light from the door, his on the bottom and hers on top, neat as a stack of mail.

body.text: “This is the daylight column,” she says. “At night. It’s a technicality.”
body.else: “This is daylight,” she says. “I’m told it’s good for you.”

body: “You just got clean,” she says. “I’m keeping my hands where your priest can see them.” She lifts the stack into the light, for the street and the party and the kid going by on a beach cruiser with a speaker in his basket, and sets it back down.

Her knee, through the ski jacket and his jeans, is the only other part of her touching him. He knows where it is at all times. He has wanted to kiss her since the foot of the steps, and all of the wanting has gone down into his hands, and she has his hands.

body.text: He tells her what he promised behind the screen: not this week. She hears it out with her eyes on his. “This week,” she says. “I heard you. I’m the week.” She takes her hands back and sits on them, both of them, bolt upright on the swing like a girl in the front pew, until he laughs. She gives them back.
body.else: She asks nothing about the confessional. She asks if he ate. “There was a Clif bar,” he says. “Around four.” “That’s a wrapper with ambitions.” From the far end of the swing she produces a paper plate with another paper plate upside down on it, and under that half a quesadilla Tomás made at seven, cold now and stiff as a shingle. He eats it in four bites with one hand, because she won’t give him back the other.

body: He tells her about the pitch. Theo on his feet in his own room with the speaker going, drawing a whiteboard in the air and wiping it off with his sleeve. The Quarter on a Sunday night. Kevin’s mother’s Odyssey, sixty-one dollars a head. Hale, who supposedly wants four thousand words on the theology of the second line. Thirty hours in a van. He leaves out who else is in the van.
Her thumb has been going back and forth across his knuckles since he sat down. Somewhere around the van it stopped.
“He drew it in the air,” she says. “The board.”
“And wiped it off.”
“With the sleeve. That’s his father. His father does that in every room he’s ever walked into.” She shakes her head at the yard. “What did he close on?”
“A favor. He said he needed me there.”
Skye whistles, low, through her teeth. “He saved the ask for last. You always close on the ask. Ted’s been in rooms.” She looks at him. “And?”
“I said no.”
The thumb starts again.
“Okay. My turn.” She sits up straighter, which on a swing takes both feet. “I got a pilot.”
“Skye.”
“The network’s sister studio. They want a girl who can play nineteen and look like she’s never been on television.” She points at herself with their stacked hands. “So, obviously.”
“You’re nineteen.”

“That’s what I said. They said, *exactly*.” The swing creaks. “It shoots in Vancouver. The Olympics have every hotel in the city, so they’re putting us in Burnaby, which is where Vancouver keeps its soundstages and its Best Westerns. I fly Friday morning. Two weeks.”
Under hers his hands close on their own, and she pats them back open like a dog she’s teaching to stay.

“It’s a pilot,” she says. “It’s nothing. It’s fourteen hours a day in a trailer for four minutes on camera, and a hotel bar full of network men saying *love it* about things they don’t. Pilot season is a cattle call where the cattle have agents.”
“You want it.”
“I want it,” she says, and looks a little surprised at herself.

“Come to Vancouver,” she says, and goes soft-focus, a tourism-board voice with a fleece on. “It rains. There are mountains, allegedly; no one living has seen them. You could hold a boom mic. You’d be a terrible boom operator. You’d lean in.”
He has Hale at one on Monday. She has a call sheet. The bit runs out down the steps and off along Del Playa after the kid on the cruiser, and she watches it go.

“So I won’t be here anyway,” she says. “Go. Go watch your Saints win. The Colts are favored by six; I looked it up; I took notes. You already listened to the last one on Tomás’s radio on these steps because of me. I’m not taking the Super Bowl off you too. Bring me back something terrible.” She squeezes his hands. “Who knows, maybe it’ll be good for you guys.”
She says it easily, to his face, in the yellow light, her thumb going steady across his knuckles in time with the record.
He tells himself it’s the Saints, and only the Saints.

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Seventeen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone. The day after Christmas my whole family watched season two of her show. She was eighteen, in a blazer, on a dock. She’s good — Dad said so, and she says nobody says good. Nonna prays for Cassidy now. She bought Chesterton used on Ventura without knowing it was my book, and wants to know who picked midnight. The Monday after Christmas she called, and we talked till my phone died. New Year’s Eve she watched my ball drop on the East Coast feed at nine her time and texted, so she’d be at midnight with me. Then she had her own, at three in the morning mine, from a locked den in the hills. I told her I called Ted *Ted*. She says he’s right: that one’s hers. She has my flight home written on her hand. She read Matthew 2 because I said Sunday was Epiphany; Herod is a jealous showrunner. OFFICIALLY, in eyeliner, on a sign at the rope at Santa Barbara, in sunglasses at night. A girl from my flight filmed it, and by morning it was on a gossip blog. Skye put the still on her own Facebook herself. Her people wanted lunch: her mother, Debbie, who manages her, and her publicist, Corinne. The rules: no pictures, ‘a friend from school,’ February. Take the airport down. She took it down. There was a folder with my last name on it, and she pushed it back without opening it. At a gas station in Buellton she took the first picture of the two of us herself, at arm’s length, and put it up instead. Then she changed her status herself and made me say yes to it on her phone — the first thing anybody ever watched her do that nobody wrote. Monday she came to the Fishbowl and argued with me about a rose. My pie got her out of remedial math. Tuesday she taught me stick in an empty lot — a voice for every stall. I do a bad Frank. We argued Conan. She posted a picture of me stalling. The radio, at 2:31: Haiti. At midnight she took the picture down — not for Corinne. Wednesday in the Brick she explained the plates under Haiti from her Oceanography book, read me Milton off the front of *Frankenstein*, and fell asleep on my shoulder. At the Haiti table she borrowed Becca’s apron and was Cassidy for twenty dollars a name, and asked me where God was at 4:53. Met Laney. Met everybody. Corinne wanted a statement; she told her the girl at the table was right about the pictures, and hung up. That night she asked me to say one for them, from her. ‘Saturday.’ Thursday Margot interviewed her at the Anchor; she says I’m the same in every room. Saturday at dawn she taught me again, inside the Point. Still very bad at it. She posted it and kept it up. She came to Sully’s and learned the Who Dat. Laney took a shot at her; she had it handled, she says, and I didn’t let her finish, and she says she’ll reward that sort of behavior. In the Saab I told her some about Lena — that we were close in the fall. She said she can tell there’s a rest. She drove me to confession, and went back to Sully’s without me. Saturday night she read me Sunday’s Gospel off her phone. Three nights in LA: a fitting for the wedding episode — she’s not the bride, she checked. Tuesday she made me explain Massachusetts while I walked. The tornado took Sol’s swing. Wednesday she drove home with the top down in the rain and put the two of us up on Facebook, soaked. Thursday we argued the Supreme Court under one umbrella until it turned inside out. She’s been a corporation since she was twelve — Skylark Pictures; her mother named it. She wrote my brother, in capitals; Rudy says write the number big. Friday the sun came out, and she called the telethon as Skylark. Saturday she drove six hours to the Walk for Life, walked the whole thing arguing with me, and stood in front of Clare when a man started screaming. Sunday she came to Mass. I told her why I didn’t go up. Out past the break I told her what I know about the basement, which isn’t much, and about Nonna’s question and Danny’s. She’s the answer to both. She knows there’s more; she said that’s enough. She asked me to teach her Nonna’s prayer. Monday a blog found the back of my head; Gina knew Danny’s jacket before the commenters did. Corinne called her at six: every picture of us down until there’s a strategy. At noon in her room I was the one who didn’t want to stop, and she stopped it — for Sunday. She’d read up on confession to do it: I can’t walk in on Wednesday with a plan, and she won’t be my plan. Ask her again after she’s watched me go up. She asked me what I lose when I sit in the pew, and I told her: they pass the plate over you. She watched them do it on Sunday and didn’t know what she was watching. Then she took a picture of us without looking, and that night she put it up, captioned with Corinne’s own rule — *my friend from school.* At the lunch in Studio City her shoes stayed on. When they got to Danny she came back for that and nothing else, and said his number from memory. In the car she said she’s very good at fine. She heard me tell Ma *tomorrow*, and that I think she’s the answer, and took the picture down at the Las Posas exit without a word. Sol’s swing is up. I told her I don’t care, and she could tell. She’s stopping anyway. She wants Nonna to like her. Wednesday she said Theo and Laney were running lines. Wednesday night she was at the curb when I got home from confession. She asked if I went. Then, in the middle of a bit about a Supreme Court justice, I said it first. I didn’t know I was going to. She’d been carrying it since Monday, and she was going to say it first. She said it back. Thursday she took me to a fundraiser in the Palisades and never said what for — it didn’t occur to her anybody would mind. It was for Boxer: Corinne wanted me in the picture so the march would stop being a story. She saw my face across the room and asked twice. I told her it was fine — she came to my Walk and took the other side seriously, so I could stand in hers. So she went back in and got the whole room to argue with me, the real arguments, in Gil’s living room, for two hours, and made sure every one of them knew where I stand. We stayed till the end. At a taquería at the bottom of Sunset she wouldn’t post Corinne’s picture. She blew me a raspberry and posted one of us at the table instead: we agree on each other, and we’re not just friends from school. She’s a union member. Two of them. Her father was Pat Doyle, a juicer on the Meridian lots, gone since she was four. Then she said her name. Mary Catherine Callender-Doyle. Baptized at St. Mary’s in Lancaster, named for his mother. The only name she has that her mother didn’t give her. I sent the first two to Gina for Nonna. At three in the morning I made the picture my profile picture. She says I stole her art. She says happy looks good on me. Friday she argued Margot to a draw and went home to learn lines. Saturday at the Point I told her Nonna lit a candle for Maria Caterina. Saturday night on the bluff she kept her word: tomorrow. Sunday she sat in the same pew, in a cardigan she bought for Mass, and watched me go up, and knelt. That night she asked first, before anything. I told her it’s still no, for now. And that it’s closer than it’s ever been. She asked what question she’s the answer to. I told her Nonna asked me what makes me pray. She asked if she does. Yes. She wants to be the good thing, with the lights off. I stayed. Just sleep. Monday she picked Danny’s birthday book on State Street — O’Connor, all the stories — and wrote the card herself, in capitals. She says Gretta’s the only one at that party who isn’t acting. At a red light the radio played it, the day before his birthday, and we sang it at each other with the top down. Somebody filmed it. Tuesday her people were on the phone by six. She didn’t share it; she wrote on my wall instead: bring the clean version next time. I told her I was sorry about her job. She kissed me on the Morro steps in front of everybody and told me never to apologize for making her happy. Then Danny called on his birthday and she got on the phone. She told him I tricked her. Then she told him the truth: she was about to leave when I walked over, and she still has the book, with CON crossed out. Candlemas she held my candle while I knelt. That night she came up to my room for the first time. I don’t know that I’d have said no. She didn’t ask. When she asks again, she says, she wants me to have nowhere to be in the morning. She asked if there’s a version of later she’s in. Wednesday on the swing, coats on, she kept me in the daylight. She’s in Vancouver for two weeks, a pilot, from Friday. She told me to go to New Orleans and watch my Saints win. Maybe it’ll be good for you guys, she said. I said yes.

choices.key: On the swing Skye told you to go to New Orleans: she’s in Vancouver anyway — maybe it’ll be good for you guys. You said yes, for Theo. He asked.
response: “Ted asked,” she says. “Ted’s never asked anybody for anything. Go.” She wants a doubloon, a real one, off a float, caught by him personally, and a T-shirt so terrible she can’t wear it outside the house. He promises both.

She leans over the stack of hands and kisses him, small and closed, a kiss built to be over fast, and it doesn’t end where she built it to. It opens a little, and stays, and she’s the one who sits back, with her eyebrows up at herself. The chains creak and settle. Inside, the needle lifts off the end of the side, and Tomás turns the record over.

choices.text: “For the Saints. And your terrible T-shirt.”
choices.key: On the swing Skye told you to go to New Orleans: she’s in Vancouver anyway — maybe it’ll be good for you guys. You said yes, for the Saints and a terrible T-shirt.
response: “For the Saints,” he says. “And your terrible T-shirt.”
“The worst one,” she says. “Sequins. A pun. A crawfish in some kind of situation.” And a doubloon, which can’t be bought; it has to be thrown at him, and he has to catch it.

The kiss starts out decent enough to show a priest and runs long, her fingers tightening on his in the stack until he can feel her rings. When she sits away she reaches up and pulls his collar straight, which it already was.

choices.key: On the swing Skye told you to go to New Orleans: she’s in Vancouver anyway — maybe it’ll be good for you guys. You said yes because she told you to.
response: “Because you told me to,” he says.
She looks at him a long time in the light from the door. “Then I’m telling you,” she says. “Go.” A doubloon, and the worst T-shirt in Louisiana.

She kisses him with their hands still stacked on her knees, a kiss she starts like a promise and can’t keep short, and when it’s over she doesn’t sit back. She leans her forehead against his, and they stay that way on the swing, breathing, while the man on the record finishes the song.

s13l.slug: WEDNESDAY · 8:50 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE LOT UNDER THE BELL TOWER
s13l.music: Townes Van Zandt — “If I Needed You”
body: The Saab comes up the hill in ten minutes, headlights swinging across the olive trees, and noses in under the bell tower where the light over the hall door can reach it. The tower goes up into the dark above it, the bell a black shape at the top. Behind the blue glass of the church one red point is burning, the lamp by the tabernacle, and nothing else.

He gets in. The top is up and the heater is going hard, and the car smells like her shampoo and hot dust off the vents and a cold coffee in the cupholder. Her iPod is propped against the windshield, its cord running down into a cassette adapter in the tape deck, and out of the speakers, turned low, comes one man and a guitar, singing like he’s been up all night and doesn’t mind.

Skye is in a gray hoodie with her hair clipped up. Both her hands are on the wheel, though the car is in park and facing a wall, and they’re all he can look at: the rings, the bones of the wrists, the knuckles going pale when she grips. She catches him looking and grips harder.

body.text: “This is the daylight column,” she says. “At night. It’s a technicality.”
body.else: “This is daylight,” she says. “I’m told it’s good for you.”

body: “You just got clean,” she says. “I’m keeping my hands on the wheel where your priest can see them.”
The gearshift stands up out of its leather boot by his knee. She tips her chin at it. “And this is Sister Mary Gearshift. She’ll be chaperoning.”
“We’ve met,” Jack says. He has the bruise.
“She’s very strict. The Carmelites let her go.” Skye lowers her voice. “Not flexible.”

body.text: When he tells her what he promised behind the screen — not this week — she hears it out with her eyes on the bell tower. “This week,” she says. “I heard you. I’m the week.” She takes her hands off the wheel and sits on them, both, very upright, a girl in the front pew, until he laughs. The hands go back on the wheel.
body.else: She asks nothing about the confessional. She asks if he ate. “There was a Clif bar.” “When?” “Four.” Without looking she reaches into the back with her right hand, keeping her left on the wheel on principle, and comes up with a white paper bag gone see-through at the bottom: half a burrito from the truck by the gas station, in foil, warm from riding on the floor vent. He eats it over the bag while she watches every bite.

body: He tells her about 412 at half past three. The music on and the desk cleared and Theo standing up, pitching him New Orleans as a studio picture: the Quarter on Sunday night; Kevin’s mother’s Odyssey; sixty-one dollars each, which is not math; Hale’s blessing for four thousand words on the second line, which is not Hale. Thirty hours in a van. He doesn’t say who else is riding.

Partway through she reaches down and turns the key back, and the engine shudders and stops. “This car drinks,” she says. With the heater off the windshield starts to go white, on her side only. She’s doing most of the breathing in here.
Her hands are at the bottom of the wheel, turning it a little on the leather, back and forth, as far as it goes in park. At *thirty hours* they stopped turning.
“He did the board?” she says. “In the air?”
“Erased it with his sleeve.”
“That’s his father’s. I’ve watched his father do that since I was a kid.” She taps the wheel with her rings. “What did he close on?”
“A favor. He said he needed me there.”
“He held the ask till the last scene,” she says, and nods slowly at the bell tower. “That’s a good room. That’s a very good room. And?”
“I said no.”
The hands start turning the wheel again.
“Okay. I’ve got one.” She drums the top of the wheel. “I got a pilot.”
“Skye.”
“The network’s sister studio. They want a girl who can play nineteen and look like she’s never been on television. So, obviously.”
“You’re nineteen.”

“You sound like the casting director.” The fog has reached the middle of her side. “It shoots in Vancouver. The Olympics have every hotel in the city, so they’re putting us in Burnaby, which is where Vancouver keeps its soundstages. I fly Friday morning. Two weeks.”
Jack looks at the bell tower, and then at her.
“It’s a pilot,” she says. “Pilots die. Nine out of ten, they shoot it, they test it on strangers in a mall in Burbank, and a man in a ponytail says no.”
“You want it.”
“I want it.” She says it again, quieter, to see if it’s still true. “I want it.”
“Come to Vancouver,” she says. “Stow away. I’ll pack you in my big suitcase. You’ll fold right up. Catholic spine; it bends at the knee.”
He has Hale on Monday at one. She has a call sheet with her name on it at five-forty in the morning. She takes the suitcase back with a little nod, as if he’d said so.

“So I won’t be here,” she says. “Go. Go watch your Saints win. The Colts are favored by six; I asked Tomás, and he had to go lie down. You already gave me the last one. Bring me back something terrible.”
She takes her hands off the wheel then, the only time, and takes his face in them, palms warm from the vents, and looks at him under the hall light.
“Who knows,” she says, “maybe it’ll be good for you guys.”
She lets go and puts her hands back on the wheel, at the bottom, where they were.
It’s the Saints, he tells himself; it’s only the Saints.

Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Seventeen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone. The day after Christmas my whole family watched season two of her show. She was eighteen, in a blazer, on a dock. She’s good — Dad said so, and she says nobody says good. Nonna prays for Cassidy now. She bought Chesterton used on Ventura without knowing it was my book, and wants to know who picked midnight. The Monday after Christmas she called, and we talked till my phone died. New Year’s Eve she watched my ball drop on the East Coast feed at nine her time and texted, so she’d be at midnight with me. Then she had her own, at three in the morning mine, from a locked den in the hills. I told her I called Ted *Ted*. She says he’s right: that one’s hers. She has my flight home written on her hand. She read Matthew 2 because I said Sunday was Epiphany; Herod is a jealous showrunner. OFFICIALLY, in eyeliner, on a sign at the rope at Santa Barbara, in sunglasses at night. A girl from my flight filmed it, and by morning it was on a gossip blog. Skye put the still on her own Facebook herself. Her people wanted lunch: her mother, Debbie, who manages her, and her publicist, Corinne. The rules: no pictures, ‘a friend from school,’ February. Take the airport down. She took it down. There was a folder with my last name on it, and she pushed it back without opening it. At a gas station in Buellton she took the first picture of the two of us herself, at arm’s length, and put it up instead. Then she changed her status herself and made me say yes to it on her phone — the first thing anybody ever watched her do that nobody wrote. Monday she came to the Fishbowl and argued with me about a rose. My pie got her out of remedial math. Tuesday she taught me stick in an empty lot — a voice for every stall. I do a bad Frank. We argued Conan. She posted a picture of me stalling. The radio, at 2:31: Haiti. At midnight she took the picture down — not for Corinne. Wednesday in the Brick she explained the plates under Haiti from her Oceanography book, read me Milton off the front of *Frankenstein*, and fell asleep on my shoulder. At the Haiti table she borrowed Becca’s apron and was Cassidy for twenty dollars a name, and asked me where God was at 4:53. Met Laney. Met everybody. Corinne wanted a statement; she told her the girl at the table was right about the pictures, and hung up. That night she asked me to say one for them, from her. ‘Saturday.’ Thursday Margot interviewed her at the Anchor; she says I’m the same in every room. Saturday at dawn she taught me again, inside the Point. Still very bad at it. She posted it and kept it up. She came to Sully’s and learned the Who Dat. Laney took a shot at her; she had it handled, she says, and I didn’t let her finish, and she says she’ll reward that sort of behavior. In the Saab I told her some about Lena — that we were close in the fall. She said she can tell there’s a rest. She drove me to confession, and went back to Sully’s without me. Saturday night she read me Sunday’s Gospel off her phone. Three nights in LA: a fitting for the wedding episode — she’s not the bride, she checked. Tuesday she made me explain Massachusetts while I walked. The tornado took Sol’s swing. Wednesday she drove home with the top down in the rain and put the two of us up on Facebook, soaked. Thursday we argued the Supreme Court under one umbrella until it turned inside out. She’s been a corporation since she was twelve — Skylark Pictures; her mother named it. She wrote my brother, in capitals; Rudy says write the number big. Friday the sun came out, and she called the telethon as Skylark. Saturday she drove six hours to the Walk for Life, walked the whole thing arguing with me, and stood in front of Clare when a man started screaming. Sunday she came to Mass. I told her why I didn’t go up. Out past the break I told her what I know about the basement, which isn’t much, and about Nonna’s question and Danny’s. She’s the answer to both. She knows there’s more; she said that’s enough. She asked me to teach her Nonna’s prayer. Monday a blog found the back of my head; Gina knew Danny’s jacket before the commenters did. Corinne called her at six: every picture of us down until there’s a strategy. At noon in her room I was the one who didn’t want to stop, and she stopped it — for Sunday. She’d read up on confession to do it: I can’t walk in on Wednesday with a plan, and she won’t be my plan. Ask her again after she’s watched me go up. She asked me what I lose when I sit in the pew, and I told her: they pass the plate over you. She watched them do it on Sunday and didn’t know what she was watching. Then she took a picture of us without looking, and that night she put it up, captioned with Corinne’s own rule — *my friend from school.* At the lunch in Studio City her shoes stayed on. When they got to Danny she came back for that and nothing else, and said his number from memory. In the car she said she’s very good at fine. She heard me tell Ma *tomorrow*, and that I think she’s the answer, and took the picture down at the Las Posas exit without a word. Sol’s swing is up. I told her I don’t care, and she could tell. She’s stopping anyway. She wants Nonna to like her. Wednesday she said Theo and Laney were running lines. Wednesday night she was at the curb when I got home from confession. She asked if I went. Then, in the middle of a bit about a Supreme Court justice, I said it first. I didn’t know I was going to. She’d been carrying it since Monday, and she was going to say it first. She said it back. Thursday she took me to a fundraiser in the Palisades and never said what for — it didn’t occur to her anybody would mind. It was for Boxer: Corinne wanted me in the picture so the march would stop being a story. She saw my face across the room and asked twice. I told her it was fine — she came to my Walk and took the other side seriously, so I could stand in hers. So she went back in and got the whole room to argue with me, the real arguments, in Gil’s living room, for two hours, and made sure every one of them knew where I stand. We stayed till the end. At a taquería at the bottom of Sunset she wouldn’t post Corinne’s picture. She blew me a raspberry and posted one of us at the table instead: we agree on each other, and we’re not just friends from school. She’s a union member. Two of them. Her father was Pat Doyle, a juicer on the Meridian lots, gone since she was four. Then she said her name. Mary Catherine Callender-Doyle. Baptized at St. Mary’s in Lancaster, named for his mother. The only name she has that her mother didn’t give her. I sent the first two to Gina for Nonna. At three in the morning I made the picture my profile picture. She says I stole her art. She says happy looks good on me. Friday she argued Margot to a draw and went home to learn lines. Saturday at the Point I told her Nonna lit a candle for Maria Caterina. Saturday night on the bluff she kept her word: tomorrow. Sunday she sat in the same pew, in a cardigan she bought for Mass, and watched me go up, and knelt. That night she asked first, before anything. I told her it’s still no, for now. And that it’s closer than it’s ever been. She asked what question she’s the answer to. I told her Nonna asked me what makes me pray. She asked if she does. Yes. She wants to be the good thing, with the lights off. I stayed. Just sleep. Monday she picked Danny’s birthday book on State Street — O’Connor, all the stories — and wrote the card herself, in capitals. She says Gretta’s the only one at that party who isn’t acting. At a red light the radio played it, the day before his birthday, and we sang it at each other with the top down. Somebody filmed it. Tuesday her people were on the phone by six. She didn’t share it; she wrote on my wall instead: bring the clean version next time. I told her I was sorry about her job. She kissed me on the Morro steps in front of everybody and told me never to apologize for making her happy. Then Danny called on his birthday and she got on the phone. She told him I tricked her. Then she told him the truth: she was about to leave when I walked over, and she still has the book, with CON crossed out. Candlemas she held my candle while I knelt. That night she came up to my room for the first time. I don’t know that I’d have said no. She didn’t ask. When she asks again, she says, she wants me to have nowhere to be in the morning. She asked if there’s a version of later she’s in. Wednesday she drove up to St. Brendan’s and sat with me in the Saab under the bell tower with the heater on and her hands where Osei could see them. She’s in Vancouver for two weeks, a pilot, from Friday. She told me to go to New Orleans and watch my Saints win. Maybe it’ll be good for you guys, she said. I said yes.

choices.key: In the Saab under the bell tower Skye told you to go to New Orleans: she’s in Vancouver anyway — maybe it’ll be good for you guys. You said yes, for Theo. He asked.
response: “Ted asked,” she tells the windshield. “Ted has never asked anybody for anything in his life. Go.” A doubloon, caught off a float with his own two hands, and a T-shirt so terrible she’ll have to sleep in it. He promises.

She leans across Sister Mary Gearshift with her hands still on the wheel and kisses him, a quick, decent, church-parking-lot kiss that doesn’t stay quick, that goes on until the gearshift finds his bruise. When she sits back she turns the key. The engine catches, the heater comes up, the fog starts to pull back off her side of the glass, and she leaves it in park.

choices.text: “For the Saints. And your terrible T-shirt.”
choices.key: In the Saab under the bell tower Skye told you to go to New Orleans: she’s in Vancouver anyway — maybe it’ll be good for you guys. You said yes, for the Saints and a terrible T-shirt.
response: “For the Saints,” he says. “And your terrible T-shirt.”
“The worst one. Sequins. A pun. A pelican in sunglasses.” And a doubloon, which he can’t buy; it has to be thrown at him from a float, and he has to catch it.

She kisses him across the gearshift with both hands on the wheel, which turns out to be worse, in the best way, than if she’d used them. When she sits back she reaches up to the fogged glass on her side and, with one fingertip, draws a fleur-de-lis: three petals and a band across the middle, the left one a little fat.

choices.key: In the Saab under the bell tower Skye told you to go to New Orleans: she’s in Vancouver anyway — maybe it’ll be good for you guys. You said yes because she told you to.
response: “Because you told me to,” he says.
She looks at him a long time under the hall light. “Then I’m telling you,” she says. “Go.” A doubloon, and the worst T-shirt in the state of Louisiana.

She leans across the gearshift with her hands still on the wheel and kisses him, slow, a kiss with somewhere it has to be and no intention of getting there on time. When it’s over she doesn’t sit back. She rests her forehead against his across the gearshift, and they stay like that, while the white comes in from the corners of her side of the glass and the song plays out low through the tape deck.
